canonical_topic: Base gas (cushion gas) versus working gas
definition: Extractable gas in a storage facility is split into base gas, which maintains enough pressure to withdraw gas at a reasonable rate and is rarely removed, and working gas, which is the gas normally injected and withdrawn for supply/demand balancing.
core_idea: Because withdrawal speed depends on the pressure differential between the facility and the pipeline, operators must trade off holding a larger working-gas volume that can only be withdrawn slowly against a smaller volume that can be withdrawn quickly, using base gas to sustain that pressure.
key_points: Gas withdrawal speed depends on the relative pressure between the storage facility and the pipeline; withdrawal is easy when the facility is nearly full and gets progressively slower as pressure drops.
Base (cushion) gas exists to maintain enough pressure to extract working gas at a reasonable speed and is rarely removed during normal operation.
During peak demand, some base gas can be removed and delivered as working gas, but doing so lowers facility pressure and slows future withdrawal rates.
Operators generally keep a fixed base gas cushion over the long run to meet performance (withdrawal rate) targets.
relationships: Determines a facility's usable capacity and withdrawal-rate performance
trading_implications: The tradeoff between working gas volume and withdrawal speed affects how much gas a facility can reliably supply during peak demand, which factors into storage valuation.
caveats: Base gas is not simply unusable dead space — it can be tapped during peak demand, but at the cost of degraded future withdrawal performance.
